title: The Watermelon Mountain Mystery
subtitle: A Sandia Mountains Mystery
story:
Chelsie pressed her forehead against the window of the Sandia Peak Tramway and watched Albuquerque shrink beneath her like a toy city. The cable car climbed higher and higher, until desert gave way to snow-dusted pines and granite cliffs that glowed faintly pink.

"Sharkie, are you watching?" she whispered, holding up her favorite stuffed shark. Sharkie’s stitched grin looked extra wide, like even he couldn’t believe the view.

At the top, Chelsie stepped into ankle-deep snow and laughed out loud. Daddio was reading a sign: SANDIA CREST — 10,678 FEET.

"Did you know Sandia means watermelon?" he said.

Chelsie squinted at the mountainside — pink granite, green juniper — and suddenly the name made perfect sense. She crunched through the snow in wide circles, arms out, Sharkie tucked under her arm.

But the mountain was only one chapter. Earlier that week, she’d stood mesmerized at the aquarium, watching seahorses drift like tiny enchanted horses, then gasping as a shark glided through the tunnel tank, slow and magnificent. "That’s your cousin," she’d whispered to Sharkie.

There was the evening they discovered birria pizza, cheese pulling in long strings while consommé dripped down their chins. The morning she found a spray mop and spent a gleeful half hour mopping every tile, announcing she’d found her "true calling." The afternoon she sat cross-legged eating a perfect cheese quesadilla with hand-made potato chips, golden and salty and still warm.

But her favorite part came at night. The Airbnb had an enormous skylight, and after the fire burned low, everyone would lie back and watch the stars appear one by one. Chelsie held Sharkie on her chest and felt thankful — for the trip, for the stars, for the time they all got to spend together.

Now, standing at 10,678 feet, she tried to memorize it all. The seahorses, the shark’s shadow, the cheese pull, the mop handle, the stars through the skylight.

"The best souvenirs aren’t things you buy," she told Sharkie softly, watching the last light turn the snow to rose gold. "They’re the things you notice."

Daddio put his arm around her shoulder. "Ready to head down?"

Chelsie took one more look. She wanted to remember everything.
lesson: The best souvenirs aren’t things you buy — they’re things you notice.
